# Final project {#sec-m5-projeto}

The final project is an **HTML accessibility report**, made in Quarto, for one of five
cities: **Belo Horizonte, Fortaleza, Porto Alegre, Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo**. It brings together what
was seen in the course: public data, spatial operations, routing with `r5r`,
accessibility measures and interactive maps with `mapgl`.

You choose the city, run the multimodal routing chapter (@sec-m4-r5r) with its data and
build the report with the blocks on this page. The page's example is Fortaleza, the same city as in the
chapter; for the other four, only what is indicated at each step changes.

There is no submission or grading: the project is yours. The idea is that you finish the course with a
document that could, with small adjustments, become a product of the Undersecretariat, and with a workflow
that works for any city with open GTFS.

## The question

**How much does cutting the bus routes with the least service reduce access to jobs in the city, and
who loses most?**

The scenario is the same in all five cities: remove from the network the quarter of the routes with the fewest trips in the
GTFS. With the same question and the same method, reports from different cities can be
compared with one another.

## The steps

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["<b>1. Data</b><br/>city package:<br/>GTFS, OpenStreetMap<br/>and land use (aopdata)"]
  B["<b>2. Routing</b><br/>r5r chapter:<br/>isochrones, itinerary,<br/>matrices and scenario"]
  C["<b>3. Report</b><br/>blocks on this page:<br/>relatorio.qmd → HTML"]
  A -- "dados/brutos/projeto_final/{cidade}/" --> B
  B -- "dados/projeto_final/" --> C
```

| Step | What to do | Where | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1. Data | download and extract the city package | below | `dados/brutos/projeto_final/{cidade}/` |
| 2. Routing | run `scripts/m4-05-r5r.R` with the city's lines | @sec-m4-r5r | `dados/projeto_final/*.rds` |
| 3. Report | stack the blocks in a `relatorio.qmd` and render | this page | `relatorio.html` |

## Step 1: the city's data

Each city has a `.7z` package, in the [`dados-modulo5` Release](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/tag/dados-modulo5) of the course repository, with everything routing needs, already checked in `r5r`. Download only the one for the city you choose (the links are in the table below):

- **`{cidade}.osm.pbf`**: the OpenStreetMap road network, cut from Geofabrik's regional extract
  around the urban area (the populated hexagons, with a 10 km margin);
- **`gtfs_{cidade}.zip`**: the public transport GTFS, in a single file;
- **`aop_{cidade}.rds`**: `aopdata`'s hexagonal grid (Ipea), with population, jobs and income
  of each hexagon;
- **`LEIA-ME.txt`** (README, in Portuguese): the sources, the GTFS validity, the recommended departure date and
  notes on the data.

| City | Package | Populated hexagons | GTFS | Watch out |
|:--|:--|--:|:--|:--|
| Belo Horizonte | [`belo_horizonte.7z`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/download/dados-modulo5/belo_horizonte.7z) (44 MB) | 2,548 | SUMOB, conventional and supplementary, until 31/12/2026 | no metro |
| Fortaleza | [`fortaleza.7z`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/download/dados-modulo5/fortaleza.7z) (62 MB) | 2,185 | Etufor, from 03/04 to 03/07/2026 | only has trips on **Saturdays and Sundays** |
| Porto Alegre | [`porto_alegre.7z`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/download/dados-modulo5/porto_alegre.7z) (40 MB) | 3,216 | EPTC, from 12/09 to 12/12/2025 | **expired** GTFS: use the October 2025 date; no Trensurb |
| Rio de Janeiro | [`rio_de_janeiro.7z`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/download/dados-modulo5/rio_de_janeiro.7z) (59 MB) | 6,392 | SMTR, bus and BRT, until 2027 | no metro, trains, light rail or ferries; trips only from 5:00 to 11:00 |
| São Paulo | [`sao_paulo.7z`](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/download/dados-modulo5/sao_paulo.7z) (175 MB) | 9,704 | SPTrans, with metro and CPTM, until 2027 | the heaviest network; trips only from 5:00 to 11:00 |

To prepare the data:

1. **Download the package** for your city, clicking on the file name in the table above or in the
   *Assets* list on the
   [Release](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/tag/dados-modulo5) page.
2. **Create the `projeto_final/` folder inside `dados/brutos/`**, in the course project folder
   (the one with the `curso-r-transportes.Rproj` file). The path becomes `dados/brutos/projeto_final/`.
3. **Move the `.7z` into that folder and extract it there.** On Windows, use
   [7-Zip](https://www.7-zip.org/): right-click on the file, *7-Zip* → *Extract
   here*. The package already contains the city folder, and the result looks like this (with Porto Alegre):

```
dados/brutos/projeto_final/porto_alegre/
├── aop_porto_alegre.rds
├── gtfs_porto_alegre.zip
├── LEIA-ME.txt
└── porto_alegre.osm.pbf
```

Do not unzip `gtfs_{cidade}.zip`: `r5r` reads the GTFS compressed.

The packages were built by `R/preparar_projeto_final.R`, which downloads the same data from the original
sources (Geofabrik, Mobility Database and `aopdata`) and processes the GTFS: the frequency-based timetables of
São Paulo and Rio were turned into fixed times, Belo Horizonte's two GTFS feeds were merged, and the
zero-duration trips, which `r5r` would treat as teleportation, were removed. The `LEIA-ME.txt`
says what was done for each city.

## Step 2: routing

The multimodal routing chapter (@sec-m4-r5r) does the whole calculation and saves each result in
`dados/projeto_final/`. It is written for Fortaleza; for another city, open
`scripts/m4-05-r5r.R` and replace the lines below, which are also in the package's `LEIA-ME.txt`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

Besides these lines:

- wherever `"gtfs_fortaleza.zip"` appears, use your city's GTFS (`"gtfs_porto_alegre.zip"`, for
  example);
- wherever `dados/brutos/fortaleza_cenario` appears, use `dados/brutos/{cidade}_cenario`;
- JVM memory: `-Xmx2G` is enough for Fortaleza; for the other cities, set aside more. The
  tests of all five ran with 8 GB (`options(java.parameters = "-Xmx8G")`, before loading
  `r5r`), and São Paulo, the largest network, needs it.

The object is called `messejana` in the chapter; in the other cities it holds another neighbourhood, but the name
can stay, so you do not have to change the rest of the code. The full calculation, with both matrices,
takes from 3 minutes (Fortaleza) to about 20 minutes (São Paulo).

At the end, the `dados/projeto_final/` folder should have these files:

```{r}
list.files("dados/projeto_final")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## One city at a time

The `dados/projeto_final/` folder holds the results of **one** city: running the chapter for
another overwrites the files. To do two cities, copy the folder before running the second.
:::

## Step 3: the report

1. **Create the `relatorio.qmd` file in the root of the course project**, the same folder that contains
   the `dados/` folder. The report's paths are relative to it.

2. **Copy the blocks below, in order**, pasting each one at the end of `relatorio.qmd`. The text
   blocks (those starting with `##`) are a starting point: rewrite them in your own words,
   with your city's name and with the numbers your result shows.

3. **Change the city in the setup block**: `cidade <- "fortaleza"` becomes the name of your city's
   folder (`"belo_horizonte"`, `"porto_alegre"`, `"rio_de_janeiro"` or `"sao_paulo"`). The
   other code blocks do not change.

4. **Render** with RStudio's *Render* button or, in the terminal, `quarto render relatorio.qmd`.
   Render every two or three blocks: an error is much easier to find right after
   pasting the block that caused it.

## The report, block by block

### Header

The header goes at the top of the file; replace Fortaleza with your city in the title and in the paragraph.
`embed-resources: true` puts the maps, styles and data
inside the HTML itself, and the report works when opened on any computer, including when sent
by e-mail.

```markdown
---
title: "Access to jobs in Fortaleza"
subtitle: "The effect of cutting the bus routes with the least service"
author: "Your name"
date: today
lang: en
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
    toc: true
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

This report estimates how many jobs each resident of Fortaleza can reach within 60 minutes
by public transport, today and in a scenario without the quarter of bus routes with the fewest trips,
and shows who loses most from the cut.
```

### Setup

The first code block chooses the city, loads the data and defines the two functions every
map uses. It is the only code block in which you change anything. It produces nothing
visible.

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| label: setup
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

# the city package folder: "belo_horizonte", "fortaleza", "porto_alegre",
# "rio_de_janeiro" or "sao_paulo"
cidade <- "fortaleza"
brutos <- file.path("dados/brutos/projeto_final", cidade)

pasta <- "dados/projeto_final"

# results of the multimodal routing chapter
comparacao <- readRDS(file.path(pasta, "comparacao.rds"))
cortadas   <- readRDS(file.path(pasta, "linhas_cortadas.rds"))

# aopdata's hexagonal grid, with the accessibility results for each hexagon
acesso <- readRDS(file.path(brutos, paste0("aop_", cidade, ".rds"))) |>
  dplyr::filter(P001 > 0) |>
  dplyr::select(id_hex) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326) |>
  dplyr::left_join(comparacao, by = c("id_hex" = "id"))

# empty map, framed on the data
mapa_base <- function(dados) {
  mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = dados, height = "525px")
}

# adds to the map a layer of hexagons coloured by a column, with a legend.
# Pass the same range to two layers that must be compared on the same scale
camada_hex <- function(mapa, dados, coluna, titulo, cores = c("#F7F6F2", "#E7A07A", "#7A1F0F"),
                       faixa = range(dados[[coluna]], na.rm = TRUE), visivel = TRUE) {
  valores <- seq(faixa[1], faixa[2], length.out = length(cores))

  mapa |>
    mapgl::add_fill_layer(
      id = titulo, source = dados,
      fill_color = mapgl::interpolate(column = coluna, values = valores, stops = cores),
      fill_opacity = 0.75, tooltip = coluna,
      visibility = if (visivel) "visible" else "none"
    ) |>
    mapgl::add_legend(titulo, values = round(faixa), colors = cores,
                      layer_id = titulo, add = TRUE)
}
```

### Data and method

```markdown
## Data and method

- **Road network:** OpenStreetMap, Fortaleza extract from Geofabrik.
- **Public transport:** Etufor GTFS, valid from April to July 2026.
- **Population, jobs and income:** `aopdata` (Ipea), H3 hexagonal grid, 2019 data.
- **Routing:** `r5r`, departure on a Saturday at 7:00, 60-minute window, median of the times,
  up to 20 minutes of walking at each end.
- **Indicator:** jobs accessible within 60 minutes (cumulative measure).
```

The sources, the GTFS validity and the departure date for your city are in the package's `LEIA-ME.txt`;
the day of the week also changes: Fortaleza is the only one with a Saturday.

### The public transport network

```markdown
## The public transport network

Each point is a stop; its size is the number of trips that pass through it in the GTFS.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
gtfs <- gtfstools::read_gtfs(file.path(brutos, paste0("gtfs_", cidade, ".zip")))

paradas <- gtfstools::convert_stops_to_sf(gtfs) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::count(gtfs$stop_times, stop_id, name = "viagens"), by = "stop_id")

mapa_base(paradas) |>
  mapgl::add_circle_layer(
    id = "paradas", source = paradas,
    circle_radius = mapgl::interpolate(column = "viagens", values = c(0, 1000), stops = c(1.5, 10)),
    circle_color = "#2F6B9A", circle_opacity = 0.7, tooltip = "viagens"
  )
```

### Where people live and where the jobs are

```markdown
## Where people live and where the jobs are

Switch the layer in the selector in the top-right corner.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
mapa_base(acesso) |>
  camada_hex(acesso, "populacao", "Population") |>
  camada_hex(acesso, "empregos", "Jobs", cores = c("#F7F6F2", "#7FA7C9", "#173A57"),
             visivel = FALSE) |>
  mapgl::add_layers_control(position = "top-right", collapsible = FALSE, mode = "single")
```

### How far you get from the Centre

```markdown
## How far you get from the Centre

Areas reachable from Praça do Ferreira in 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
isocronas <- readRDS(file.path(pasta, "isocronas.rds")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(isochrone))          # the smaller bands on top

cores_iso <- c("#173A57", "#2F6B9A", "#A9C4DA", "#F6DCCB")

mapa_base(isocronas) |>
  mapgl::add_fill_layer(
    id = "isocronas", source = isocronas,
    fill_color = mapgl::match_expr("isochrone", values = c(15, 30, 45, 60), stops = cores_iso),
    fill_opacity = 0.6, tooltip = "isochrone"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Minutes from the Centre", values = c(15, 30, 45, 60),
                    colors = cores_iso, type = "categorical")
```

### An example trip

```markdown
## An example trip

The fastest option from Messejana to the Centre, leg by leg.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
itinerario <- readRDS(file.path(pasta, "itinerario.rds")) |>
  dplyr::filter(option == 1)

modos <- unique(itinerario$mode)
cores_modo <- c(WALK = "#7A7A7A", BUS = "#2F6B9A", RAIL = "#C2542D", SUBWAY = "#7A1F0F",
                TRAM = "#E7A07A")[modos]

mapa_base(itinerario) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(
    id = "itinerario", source = itinerario,
    line_color = mapgl::match_expr("mode", values = modos, stops = unname(cores_modo)),
    line_width = 5, tooltip = "route"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Mode", values = modos, colors = unname(cores_modo), type = "categorical")
```

### Access to jobs today

```markdown
## Access to jobs today

How many jobs can be reached within 60 minutes by public transport, from each hexagon.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
cores_acesso <- c("#F6DCCB", "#2F6B9A", "#173A57")
faixa_acesso <- range(c(acesso$atual, acesso$cenario), na.rm = TRUE)

mapa_base(acesso) |>
  camada_hex(acesso, "atual", "Jobs within 60 min", cores = cores_acesso,
             faixa = faixa_acesso)
```

### The scenario

```markdown
## The scenario: without the routes with the least service

The scenario removes `r length(cortadas)` routes, the quarter of them with the fewest trips in the GTFS. The two
layers use the same colour scale; switch between them in the selector.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
mapa_base(acesso) |>
  camada_hex(acesso, "atual", "Current", cores = cores_acesso, faixa = faixa_acesso) |>
  camada_hex(acesso, "cenario", "Scenario", cores = cores_acesso, faixa = faixa_acesso,
             visivel = FALSE) |>
  mapgl::add_layers_control(position = "top-right", collapsible = FALSE, mode = "single")
```

### Who loses access

```markdown
## Who loses access

Change in accessible jobs with the cut: red where access is lost, blue where it is gained.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
limite <- max(abs(acesso$perda_abs), na.rm = TRUE)
cores_dif <- c("#C2542D", "#F7F6F2", "#2F6B9A")

mapa_base(acesso) |>
  mapgl::add_fill_layer(
    id = "variacao", source = acesso,
    fill_color = mapgl::interpolate(column = "perda_abs", values = c(-limite, 0, limite),
                                    stops = cores_dif),
    fill_opacity = 0.8, tooltip = "perda_abs"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Change in accessible jobs", values = round(c(-limite, 0, limite)),
                    colors = cores_dif)
```

### Who loses most

```markdown
## Who loses most

The average change for each income quintile, weighted by population (1 = the poorest 20%).
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
por_renda <- comparacao |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(renda)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    pessoas = sum(populacao),
    variacao_pct = weighted.mean(perda_pct, populacao, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = renda
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(renda)

knitr::kable(por_renda, digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Income quintile", "People", "Average change (%)"))

ggplot(por_renda, aes(factor(renda), variacao_pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#C2542D") +
  labs(x = "Income quintile (1 = poorest)",
       y = "Average change in accessible jobs (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Road network loading

```markdown
## Road network loading

The segments most used by car trips between the most populous areas and those with the most
jobs; the width is the flow.
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
carga <- readRDS(file.path(pasta, "carga.rds")) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326) |>
  dplyr::arrange(fluxo)                          # the most loaded segments on top

mapa_base(carga) |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(
    id = "carga", source = carga, line_color = "#1a5b8a", line_opacity = 0.8,
    line_width = mapgl::interpolate(column = "fluxo", values = range(carga$fluxo),
                                    stops = c(0.5, 8)),
    tooltip = "fluxo"
  )
```

### Conclusions, limitations and annex

The end of the report is your own text: what the result shows, and what it cannot show. The
limitations below are Fortaleza's. For your city, replace the first with the notes in the
`LEIA-ME.txt` (what is missing from the network, the GTFS period) and add any you find.

```markdown
## Conclusions

(Who is affected, by how much, and what this implies for the decision.)

## Limitations

- The GTFS only has weekend trips: the result holds for a Saturday morning, not for the
  peak of a weekday.
- Population, jobs and income are from 2019; the transport network is from 2026.
- The loading considers only cars and a small set of origin–destination pairs, with
  hypothetical flows.

## Annex: execution environment
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
sessionInfo()
```

## How to tell whether it came out well

| Criterion | What is expected |
|:--|:--|
| Reproducibility | someone else runs `scripts/m4-05-r5r.R` and the report from scratch and gets the same result |
| Technical correctness | a departure date with trips in the GTFS, routing parameters stated |
| Clarity of communication | maps with legends, a diverging palette for the difference, short text in each section |
| Interpretation | the text says what the result means, not what the code does |
| Limitations | the weaknesses are made explicit, not hidden |

With the package data and the step 2 parameters, `r5r` always gives the same result. The
numbers below came from the report run from scratch in all five cities (`r5r` 2.4.0); if yours
are very different, check the departure date and the GTFS:

| City | Routes cut | Change in quintile 1 (poorest) | Change in quintile 5 (richest) | Trip from the neighbourhood to the centre |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Belo Horizonte | 83 of 328 | −4.9% | −1.0% | Venda Nova → Praça Sete, 57 min |
| Fortaleza | 70 of 325 | −7.1% | −3.0% | Messejana → Praça do Ferreira, 53 min |
| Porto Alegre | 75 of 300 | −3.3% | −0.2% | Restinga → Mercado Público, 93 min |
| Rio de Janeiro | 112 of 422 | −4.5% | −4.4% | Madureira → Central do Brasil, 72 min |
| São Paulo | 297 of 1,184 | −6.2% | −3.7% | Cidade Tiradentes → Praça da Sé, 115 min |

## Going further

- **Another time cut-off:** 30 minutes instead of 60, in the `cutoff` of the multimodal routing chapter.
- **Another opportunity:** schools or health services, which `aopdata` also has.
- **Another scenario:** instead of cutting routes, increase the frequency of the trunk routes with
  `gtfstools`, and measure the gain.
- **Compare cities:** run two cities (copying `dados/projeto_final/` between one and the other) and
  put the income tables side by side. Where does the cut weigh most on the poorest?
- **A sixth city:** `R/preparar_projeto_final.R` builds the package for any city in
  `aopdata` with a GTFS in the Mobility Database. First, check that the GTFS timetables are complete:
  Curitiba was left out because its trips have no times along the route.

`mapgl` also has `compare()`, which puts two maps side by side with a swipe curtain. But it
loads a component from the internet that prevents the HTML from coming out as a single file, which is why the
report uses switchable layers.

## Results

::: {.callout-note}
## Published one week after the final project

The files in this section were released one week after the final project was due, so that
you can check your work, see what another city's report would look like or run all five.
:::

For each city there are two files (in Portuguese, like the original course):

- **the routing** (`roteamento_{cidade}.R`): the whole calculation of the multimodal routing
  chapter, with the city's parameters already filled in. It reads the city package and writes the
  intermediate results (isochrones, itinerary, compared matrices, loading) to
  `dados/projeto_final/{cidade}/`;
- **the report** (`relatorio_{cidade}.qmd`): the final report, with all the blocks on this page
  and the city's text, including the limitations and a first conclusion, written from the
  numbers.

Or download all ten at once:
[`projeto_final_resultados.zip`](../recursos/projeto_final/projeto_final_resultados.zip).

To run a city:

1. **The data:** extract the city's `.7z` package into `dados/brutos/projeto_final/`, as in
   step 1.
2. **The files:** save `roteamento_{cidade}.R` and `relatorio_{cidade}.qmd` in the **root of the
   course project**, the folder that contains `dados/`.
3. **The routing:** open `roteamento_{cidade}.R` in RStudio and click *Source*. At the end, it
   reports how many files it wrote to `dados/projeto_final/{cidade}/`. Each city has its own
   subfolder: running one does not delete the results of another, nor those of step 2.
4. **The report:** open `relatorio_{cidade}.qmd` and click *Render*. The HTML comes out next to it,
   in a single file, with the maps embedded.

The numbers should match those in the table in the "How to tell whether it came out well" section, above: with the same
data and parameters, `r5r` always gives the same result. The report needs the same as
yours: Java 21 for the routing and the module 5 packages.

The ten files come from two templates, one for the routing and another for the report. They are
filled in with each city's parameters by `R/gerar_resultados_projeto_final.R`, in the
course repository.
